rv.q: What a joy to have them back on Broadway and to think that, even half-dead, they’re unkillable.
"Airline Highway" feels very much like the work of a hometown writer, whose first impulse is affection and surely not cold-eyed analysis.
But like a lot of all-night parties, this one doesn’t stand up to the light.
Like the cinder-block–mounted car on the side of Scott Pask's seedy multilevel set, the play has color and beat-up charm, but doesn't go anywhere.
This is anthropology trying to disguise itself as drama and, for a while, under Joe Mantello’s relaxed direction, it’s enough.
This story has less original characters and a forced peg.
But D’Amour, while clearly sympathetic to her characters, conjures a world too neatly balanced, too eccentric, too oddly wholesome.
Many in the audience will have lost patience long before then with this disappointing play, which is a perplexing choice for nonprofit company Manhattan Theatre Club’s Broadway house.
I wish the play were as good, but it’s a wholly derivative piece of work that has been knocked together from refurbished spare theatrical parts.

“Airline Highway,” on the other hand, is overstuffed and unfocused, the plot loosely organized around the funeral party for Miss Ruby, a former burlesque queen who’s the grand elder of the Hummingbird’s ragtag community.

D'Amour does not burden her characters with pity, any more than the elderly burlesque queen who is their matriarch does. To Miss Ruby, made ravaged and regal by the great Judith Roberts, all are 'little duckies'...The playwright clearly shares Miss Ruby's compassion for her flock, and her respect for each member's individual dignity...
But though the inhabitants and visitors to the decrepit Hummingbird Motel in Lisa D’Amour’s Airline Highway may seem familiar, they still touch your heart and get under your skin.
If its characters can feel familiar, D'Amour's writing unsparingly, unabashedly gets at fundamental aspects of the human condition.

That Tanya keeps it together long enough to send off her old friend in style can be credited to the motel’s itinerant handyman Terry, a character that Tim Edward Rhoze effortlessly turns into the play’s moral compass.
The 16 performers work together so effectively in creating the community that hangs around the Hummingbird Motel, that they surely deserve a Tony Award for great ensemble acting.
They make Airline Highway more than worth a one-night stay.
MTC is giving this Steppenwolf play a splendid production, courtesy of director Joe Mantello and a thoroughly winning cast.
There aren’t any sort of tidy resolutions in “Airline Highway,” and we never get the feeling these has-beens at the Humming Bird will pay Miss Ruby any due.
But nice as it is to have a wide assortment of colorful characters, the focus too often drifts away from the central players of the plot.
Nonetheless, it may be that in the long run it signals too obliviously the pessimistic outlook on life about to unfold at length.
There's a too-colorful, almost exploitative feeling about the proceedings that is less a gut punch than a mild upset stomach.
Lisa D'Amour's script is a slow road to nowhere.
Only the fine cast saves the play from being a complete waste of time.
This fine new play is well-worth everyone's time, money and consideration.

But Airline Highway, her intriguing but diffuse new drama at Manhattan Theatre Company’s Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, is more of a soft-focus snapshot of urban poverty than the powerhouse it could have been.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this New Orleans-set ensemble drama, praising the strong cast and Joe Mantello's direction but finding D'Amour's sprawling character study aimless and populated with clichés, lacking the focus of her earlier work "Detroit."

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
